strengths: The paper targets an important and timely systems problem: serving augmented/tool-using LLMs under latency SLOs, where external-call pauses, API return lengths, and KV-cache handling create scheduling behavior that differs from ordinary LLM serving.

The design is practically motivated. The two-stage scheduler explicitly separates pre-call prediction from post-call runtime correction, and the dynamic token batching mechanism addresses a real limitation of static max-batch-token settings under changing memory pressure.

The evaluation covers multiple GPUs, two model sizes, two augmented workloads, several arrival processes, and several service metrics including goodput, TTFT, normalized latency, SLO attainment, and tail latency. The reported gains over vLLM and InferCept are large and consistent in the presented settings.
The paper includes useful empirical motivation showing FCFS head-of-line blocking, sensitivity to batch-token limits, and the importance of API return length for augmented LLM serving.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not include the most relevant scheduling baselines beyond FCFS-based vLLM/InferCept. Since the core contribution is request scheduling, comparisons to shortest-job-first/length-aware scheduling, recent learning-to-rank schedulers, output-length-prediction schedulers, or augmented-LLM scheduling work such as Fast Inference for Augmented LLMs are necessary to establish the claimed contribution. The very large gains may mostly reflect replacing FCFS with any reasonable size-aware policy.

Several methodological details are underspecified, weakening reproducibility: predictor bucket definitions, training features, hyperparameters, alpha/beta/gamma settings, target_max profiling procedure, workload preprocessing, API duration simulation or measurement, and exact implementation changes to vLLM/InferCept are not sufficiently described. No artifact or code availability is stated.

The scheduling formulation has potential correctness issues. The anti-starvation term is added to the scheduling value even though lower-cost requests appear to be prioritized; if sorting is ascending, this makes long-waiting requests less likely to run, contradicting the stated fairness goal. The paper does not resolve this ambiguity.

The cost model is not convincingly derived or validated. Several equations mix memory footprint, iteration time, and token counts in ways that are dimensionally unclear, and the scheduler's sensitivity to prediction error is only lightly addressed despite output-length accuracy being only 65% on the Merge dataset.

The paper claims adaptivity to external-call features, but Stage I prediction of API return length is not clearly specified even though return length is central to the motivation and formulas. It is unclear what is known before the API returns versus what is only available for Stage II correction.

Ablations are too limited. They show dynamic batching and scheduling together, but do not isolate Stage I vs Stage II, predictor quality, anti-starvation, context-policy interactions, or dynamic batching bounds. This makes it hard to know which components are essential.

The SLO choices strongly affect goodput, but the main results use a fixed TTFT < 1s and normalized latency < 10x iteration time with limited justification and limited sensitivity in the main text. Some reported average TTFT values are hundreds of seconds, which raises questions about overload regimes and whether the comparisons reflect practical serving configurations.

Limitations and ethics are essentially absent. While the work is a systems paper with limited direct ethical risk, it should still discuss fairness tradeoffs from prioritizing short/cheap requests, possible starvation or priority inversion, workload representativeness, and deployment constraints.

strengths: Targets an important and timely systems problem: serving tool-augmented LLM requests under SLO constraints, where external-call pauses, API return lengths, and KV-cache handling create scheduling issues not present in standard LLM serving.

The core intuition is reasonable: request scheduling should account for external-call duration, return length, context handling policy, and runtime corrections, rather than relying only on FCFS or static token limits.
The paper reports experiments across two models, multiple GPU settings, two augmented-LLM workloads, several arrival processes, and includes ablations plus burstiness/tail-latency analyses.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not sufficiently supported. The reported 4.7-33.1x gains appear to rely on weak or under-tuned baselines using FCFS and static token limits, while stronger LLM-serving schedulers discussed in related work are not implemented as baselines or combined with the same context-handling mechanisms.

The scheduling formulation has serious clarity and correctness issues. The paper says lower scheduling value means higher priority, but the anti-starvation term adds alpha times waiting time to the value, which would make long-waiting requests less likely to be scheduled if sorting ascending. This directly undermines the claimed fairness mechanism.

Several cost equations are poorly justified dimensionally and operationally. It is unclear why the proposed memory-time proxy accurately predicts queuing impact, why decode costs are formulated as shown, how constants such as alpha, beta, gamma, target_max, swap bandwidth, and iteration time are chosen, or how sensitive the system is to them.

The prediction module is underspecified. The manuscript gives only coarse BERT accuracy/MSE numbers and dataset splits, but does not make clear whether evaluation requests are held out from predictor training, how API duration is observed, how prediction errors affect scheduling, or whether online distribution shift is handled.

Reproducibility is weak: there is no code/artifact statement, insufficient implementation detail for vLLM/InferCept integration, incomplete hyperparameter settings, and limited information about workload construction, API latency simulation, batching configuration, warmup, repetitions, variance, or statistical uncertainty.

Presentation quality is poor in several places. Many figures/tables are hard to interpret from the PDF extraction, some equations are malformed or ambiguous, and the writing contains repeated grammatical errors and vague summaries instead of precise experimental interpretation.

The evaluation omits important stress cases and limitations: multi-tenant fairness, starvation/tail behavior under adversarial long jobs, real external API latency variability/failures, multiple tool calls per request, larger modern models, multi-GPU serving beyond a small setting, and the overhead/risk of preempting paused KV memory.

The paper has essentially no explicit limitations or ethics discussion. For a serving system that reorders user requests and uses learned predictors, it should discuss fairness across users/request classes, possible priority bias, and operational risks under prediction failure.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely systems problem: serving augmented/tool-calling LLMs under SLO constraints, where API pauses, return lengths, and KV-cache handling create scheduling behavior not covered well by standard LLM serving work.

The core idea is sensible and practically motivated: combine request-aware scheduling with runtime correction after tool/API return, and adapt the batch token budget based on memory/load rather than using a fixed limit.

Evaluation is fairly broad for a systems paper: two augmented-LLM datasets, multiple arrival processes, fixed-time and fixed-request workloads, several GPUs, GPT-J-6B and OPT-13B, and metrics including goodput, SLO attainment, TTFT, normalized latency, tail latency, TPOT, and ablations.
The reported gains over vLLM and InferCept are large and consistent across many settings, especially under higher load where FCFS scheduling and static token limits degrade sharply.

The paper includes useful component ablations showing that dynamic token batching helps and that the two-stage scheduler provides additional gains, with prediction overhead reported as below 1% of request completion time.
weaknesses: The strongest claims rely mainly on comparison to vLLM and InferCept, both effectively FCFS in the studied configuration. The paper cites scheduling baselines such as SJF/output-length prediction/learning-to-rank approaches but does not compare against adapted versions of them, making it hard to isolate how much of the gain is due to AugServe's specific scheduler versus any non-FCFS cost-aware scheduler.

Some algorithmic details are ambiguous or possibly inconsistent. The paper says long-waiting requests should gain priority, but the scheduling value adds a positive alpha * waiting_time term while lower scheduling values appear to be prioritized; unless sorting is descending, this would reduce priority for older requests. The sort direction and fairness mechanism need clarification.

The prediction module is under-specified for reproducibility and robustness: it reports output-length accuracy and API-duration MSE, but gives limited details on bucket definitions, features, training procedure, hyperparameters, calibration, and sensitivity to prediction error. Generalization beyond the two evaluated datasets is not established.

The workload construction is not fully transparent. It is unclear how real API/tool latency, return lengths, multi-round tool calls, and API variability are modeled or replayed, and whether external calls are actual live calls, traces, or synthetic delays. This matters because the method explicitly optimizes around API duration and return length.

The dynamic token batching mechanism depends on offline profiling parameters such as target_max, beta bounds, gamma, and safety memory, but the paper gives little guidance on tuning, stability, or portability to other models/hardware/load regimes.

Several equations and cost models are heuristic and not fully justified. For example, the cost formulas mix memory footprint, forward time, and length terms in ways that are not clearly derived or validated against measured iteration/runtime costs; this weakens the theoretical support for the scheduling score.

Presentation is generally understandable but rough in places: there are grammar issues, tiny/low-readability plots, inconsistent terminology such as normalized/normalization latency, and some extracted figure text appears problematic. These do not obscure the main idea but reduce polish.

The limitations and ethics discussion is essentially absent. The paper should more directly discuss fairness/starvation tradeoffs, workload representativeness, deployment risks of prioritizing short/cheap requests, and implications for users whose requests are systematically more expensive.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details, exact configs, seeds/repetitions, confidence intervals or variance, and code/artifact availability are not sufficiently specified. The very large speedups would be more convincing with error bars and clearer experimental recipes.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely systems problem: serving tool-augmented LLMs under SLOs, where external-call pauses interact poorly with conventional FCFS batching and KV-cache policies.

The proposed design is coherent: AugServe combines state-aware value-density scheduling, realized feedback after tool returns, INFERCEPT-style context handling, and a dynamic token budget based on both free and reclaimable memory.

The empirical evaluation is relatively broad for a systems paper, covering multiple models and hardware settings, two augmented-workload datasets, Poisson and bursty arrivals, ablations, prediction-noise sensitivity, scheduling overhead, mixed external/non-external workloads, and a larger Llama-3-70B setting.

The reported gains are substantial, especially against vLLM/INFERCEPT under high load, and the ablation suggests that state-aware scheduling is the dominant contributor while dynamic token budgeting gives complementary improvement.

The paper is generally well structured and the appendix usefully includes pseudocode, context-handling formulas, sensitivity analyses, and a scoped approximation result for the simplified greedy subproblem.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate rather than strong. The method is mainly a careful combination of known ingredients: SJF/value-density scheduling, INFERCEPT-style context handling, output/call-duration prediction, aging, and dynamic token budgets. The conceptual novelty over memory-aware SJF/MARS is plausible but not sharply isolated.

Several central experimental details are underspecified, which weakens reproducibility: the predictor training split/features, workload construction from ToolBench/INFERCEPT, exact vLLM/INFERCEPT integration changes, external-call simulation or replay mechanism, token-budget hyperparameters, and code/artifact availability are not described sufficiently.

The evaluation depends heavily on goodput under chosen SLOs, but the SLO thresholds are only lightly justified. It is unclear how sensitive the large multiplicative gains are to TTFT < 1s and normalized latency < 10x single-iteration time, especially since baselines sometimes collapse to near-zero goodput.

Fairness and starvation risks are not fully addressed. The aging term is intended to prevent starvation, but no per-class fairness, worst-case waiting-time, or long-request degradation analysis is provided, which matters for a scheduler that prioritizes high value-density short/resource-efficient work.

The comparison to MARS is relegated to the appendix and uses a reimplementation because MARS lacks a prediction model for this workload. This may be reasonable, but it leaves uncertainty about baseline fidelity and should be more central given that MARS is the closest scheduling competitor.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The approximation theorem applies only to a fixed offline knapsack subproblem and explicitly does not cover the actual online multi-stage serving problem, so it should not be read as a guarantee for AugServe as deployed.

The paper has presentation issues: many plots appear visually dense and some numeric values are hard to recover from the text; the main paper reports large geometric-mean gains without enough tabular detail to audit them. There are also minor formatting and spacing problems throughout.

The limitations and ethics discussion are thin. The impact statement is generic, and the paper does not discuss operational risks such as prioritization bias across users/classes, interactions with unreliable third-party tools, privacy implications of tool metadata used for prediction, or failure modes under distribution shift.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely systems problem: serving tool/API-augmented LLMs under latency SLOs, where pauses, KV-cache handling, and request heterogeneity can make FCFS batching inefficient.

The proposed combination of state-aware scheduling and adaptive batch-level token budgeting is directionally sensible, and the paper includes useful ablations showing that scheduling is the dominant contributor while the dynamic token budget adds incremental benefit.

The evaluation spans several model/GPU settings and reports multiple serving metrics, including goodput, TTFT, normalized latency, burstiness, mixed workloads, and a comparison to a memory-based SJF scheduler in the appendix.
weaknesses: The empirical support is not convincing enough for the central claims. The largest gains are mostly against FCFS vLLM/INFERCEPT baselines that are known to be weak for this setting; the stronger memory-aware SJF baseline is only in the appendix, appears to be a reimplementation, and is not validated against the original system or prediction setup.

Several evaluation details needed to judge soundness are underspecified: how traces are constructed, whether external calls are real or simulated, train/test splits for the BERT predictor, request length/tool-call distributions, exact SLO rationale, tuning protocol, and whether the same prediction information is available to all baselines.

The method is less technically crisp than the claims suggest. The space-time cost model is introduced as an integral over memory and time, but the actual greedy packing uses a token budget and breaks at the first infeasible request; the relationship between the objective, memory constraint, token budget, and online scheduling behavior is not rigorously established.

The predictor is a major dependency, yet the paper gives only bucket accuracy/MSE and an artificial multiplicative-noise test. This does not establish robustness to distribution shift, cold-start deployment, unseen APIs/tools, or systematic prediction errors, all of which are central in augmented LLM serving.

Theoretical analysis is weak: the appendix gives a standard simplified 1/2-approximation for an offline fixed-value/fixed-cost knapsack-like step and explicitly states it does not extend to the online multi-stage setting that the paper actually addresses.

Reproducibility is poor. I did not find an artifact, code-release statement, detailed implementation parameters, predictor training recipe, workload generation scripts, or enough system configuration detail to reproduce the reported large goodput improvements.

Presentation is polished at a high level but often overclaims. The paper repeatedly states that results validate generality and robustness, while many experiments are narrow, heavily dependent on trace/prediction assumptions, and reported mostly as aggregate curves without confidence intervals or variance.

Limitations and ethics are inadequately treated. The impact statement is generic, and the paper does not seriously discuss deployment risks such as unfairness/starvation under value-density scheduling, effects on different user classes, sensitivity to SLO choice, or operational risks from aggressive cache eviction/swapping.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely systems problem: serving tool/external-call-augmented LLMs under SLO constraints. The distinction between ordinary LLM serving and augmented serving is well motivated through the request lifecycle, HoL blocking, paused KV-cache states, and fixed token-budget issues.

The proposed design is technically coherent. Modeling request execution as multi-stage segments and using state-aware space-time costs with post-invocation runtime feedback is a sensible way to capture the main sources of heterogeneity that FCFS, length-based SJF, and memory-only scheduling miss.

The evaluation is broad and convincing for the central claims. The authors compare against vLLM, INFERCEPT, speculative SJF, and in the appendix MARS; they test multiple models and GPU settings, including GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B, Vicuna-13B, and Llama-3-70B-Instruct; and they report goodput, TTFT, normalized latency, tail latency, SLO attainment, bursty arrivals, mixed workloads, scheduling overhead, and sensitivity to prediction errors.

The reported gains are substantial: geometric-mean goodput improvements of roughly 6.5x over vLLM and 4.7x over INFERCEPT in the abstract, with large TTFT reductions. The ablations and robustness studies support the claim that the gains come mainly from reduced queuing delay and better handling of external-call-induced state changes.
The paper is generally well organized. The problem formulation, algorithm, context-handling policy equations, and appendix details make the system easier to understand and partially reproduce.
weaknesses: The main limitation is that reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript describes the implementation at a high level and gives pseudocode, datasets, models, hardware, SLO definitions, and some overhead numbers, but I did not find a clear artifact/code-release statement or enough low-level implementation detail to independently reproduce the full serving system and all baselines.

The evaluation is strong but still somewhat workload-dependent. The external-call duration and return-token distributions are drawn from INFERCEPT and ToolBench-style traces; it is less clear how AugServe behaves with real production tool APIs whose latency distributions, failures, rate limits, and dependency correlations may be more adversarial or nonstationary.

The predictor is central to initial scheduling and policy selection, but its training setup is under-specified. The paper reports bucket accuracy and MSE, and includes injected multiplicative noise experiments, but gives limited detail on train/test splits, feature construction, distribution shift, and whether prediction failures could systematically bias scheduling for certain request classes.

The theoretical guarantee is only for a simplified fixed-value, fixed-cost 0-1 knapsack abstraction and does not cover the fully dynamic setting with evolving states, prediction error, external-call returns, and bounded token-budget adaptation. This is acceptable for intuition but should not be read as a guarantee for the deployed algorithm.

The limitations and ethics discussion is perfunctory. The impact statement says no societal consequences need highlighting, but augmented LLM serving can affect cost, access, energy use, and reliability of deployed agentic systems; a more thoughtful discussion of operational risks and failure modes would improve the paper.

Some presentation details could be sharper: the paper makes many very large relative-improvement claims, but several plots are hard to parse in the PDF/text extraction, and the main paper would benefit from clearer numeric tables for the most important end-to-end results rather than relying heavily on figures and appendix discussion.
